items.caption:
The evolution of AI-generated video between 2023 and 2026 has been so drastic that it hardly feels like the same technology anymore. Just three years ago, AI videos were instantly recognizable by their distorted faces, glitchy motion, and brief, heavily flawed clips. Today, AI tools can generate scenes with impressive camera work, lighting, dynamic motion, and cinematic level detail—all from a simple text prompt or a single image.

This massive leap in such a short timeframe highlights the incredible speed of progress in the field, raising a captivating question: if we've come this far in just three years, how indistinguishable from reality will AI video be by 2029?

#aivideo #ai #technology #innovation #future

memegodMatching tattoos have become a popular trend among couples looking to show their love and dedication to one another. While some choose to ink their partner’s name, initials, or a special anniversary date, others go for creative designs that hold a deeper meaning in their relationship. For many, these tattoos represent a lifelong connection and serve as a permanent reminder of the memories and experiences they’ve shared.However, getting a tattoo dedicated to your significant other comes with some serious risks. Unlike matching clothes or accessories, tattoos don’t disappear when a relationship ends. Removing them can be costly, painful, and often takes several laser sessions. Because of this, many tattoo artists encourage couples to think twice before permanently putting someone’s name on their body. Others prefer small, subtle designs that still carry sentimental value without taking up half their chest. 😭😂View all 89 comments

items.caption:
🎬 Green Book (2018)

Two men from completely different worlds. One unforgettable road trip that challenges everything they thought they knew about each other.

Set in 1962, the film follows Tony Lip, a tough-talking Italian-American nightclub bouncer from the Bronx who takes a job driving Dr. Don Shirley, a sophisticated and exceptionally talented Black classical pianist, on a concert tour through the American South. As they travel through a deeply segregated society, their contrasting personalities, backgrounds, and beliefs lead to frequent disagreements and unexpected moments of humor. But while navigating racial prejudice, uncomfortable encounters, and the challenges of life on the road, the two gradually develop a meaningful connection that transforms their understanding of friendship, dignity, and respect.

A heartwarming biographical comedy-drama filled with outstanding performances, memorable conversations, touching moments, and a powerful exploration of racial discrimination, unlikely friendship, cultural differences, compassion, and the importance of looking beyond prejudice to discover our shared humanity.
Why does iOS feel so nice to use
items.summary: The creator investigates the secret behind iOS's smooth and intuitive feel by examining its decompiled scrolling code, revealing that it uses a capped hyperbolic function for overscroll bounce and spring-based damped harmonic motion for state changes rather than simple timelines.
items.transcript: what's fascinated me for a while is how the animations on an iPhone feel so intuitive to the touch so today I actually tried to gain an understanding of how Apple does it so I pulled the iOS 27 update found the part that controls your scrolling and turned the machine code back into readable code that everyone could understand and here are the tricks I found the first one is when you pull past the end of the page I've heard a lot of videos online claiming that it's logarithmic, but it actually isn't. It's actually this X is how far your finger is pulled, D is the height of the screen and C is constant. It's a hyperbola where the further you pull, the less it follows. And unlike a log, it has a ceiling, so you can never go past one screen no matter how far you drag. The second one is what happens when you change something that's already in motion. Most apps animate things like a toggle on timer, meaning the animations work on a set path and a set length. If you grab it halfway, the old animation gets thrown out and you start from zero. But Apple uses springs instead. It's damped harmonic motion, and it makes it feel like you're actually pulling something in your hand. Even SwiftUI's presets work like this. They're all based on springs, you're just toggling how much friction it has. I wanted to create this video because I find product human interaction an extremely interesting field. It reminds me of Jacob's law, which claims that most users spend their time on other websites, so they naturally expect your product to work like everyone else's. yeah, that's it follow for more
